events.title: The Mamertine appeal and the Roman vote for war
events.summary: The Mamertines, Campanian ex-mercenaries holding Messana and pressed by Hiero II of Syracuse, appealed to both Carthage and Rome. The Senate could not decide; the people, encouraged by the consuls with promises of plunder, voted to accept the Mamertines into alliance, beginning Rome's first war outside Italy.
events.detail: Polybius (1.10-11) says the Senate hesitated because helping the Mamertines would be inconsistent with Rome's recent punishment of the Campanian legion at Rhegium (270), but that the people, worn by war yet tempted by the consuls' promises of booty, carried the decision. A Carthaginian garrison under Hanno already sat in Messana's citadel; the Mamertines expelled it when the Roman military tribune Gaius Claudius arrived. Carthage crucified Hanno for losing the town. The decision is the classic test case for theories of Roman imperialism: Harris reads it as aggressive appetite for gloria and praeda, Hoyos as an unplanned escalation in which neither power expected a long war, Eckstein as a predictable act in an anarchic interstate system.
scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Eckstein, Mediterranean Anarchy, Interstate War, and the Rise of Rome (2006)
Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)
events.debate: Polybius (3.26) rejects the 'treaty of Philinus' that allegedly barred Rome from Sicily and Carthage from Italy; if it existed, Rome broke it in 264. Modern opinion is split (Hoyos and others take it seriously as a misunderstanding of the 306 treaty). Whether the Senate truly abdicated the decision to the people, or Polybius (via Fabius Pictor) shifts blame onto the plebs, is also debated.

events.title: Battle of Messana
events.summary: Appius Claudius Caudex ran the Carthaginian blockade of the Straits by night and defeated first Hiero and then the Carthaginian army besieging Messana, breaking their improvised alliance. It was the first Roman army ever to fight outside Italy.
events.detail: Hiero and the Carthaginians had made common cause to besiege Messana. Polybius (1.11-12) says Claudius beat the Syracusans and then the Carthaginians on successive days, after which Hiero withdrew to Syracuse. Philinus, the pro-Carthaginian historian, told it very differently, and Polybius (1.14-15) criticises both him and Fabius Pictor for partisanship; Zonaras preserves a version in which Claudius was initially repulsed. Claudius' cognomen Caudex ('blockhead' or, by an ancient etymology, 'log-boat') was later connected with ships.

battle.significance: Opened Sicily to Roman armies and broke the Syracusan-Carthaginian coalition; within a year Hiero changed sides.

events.debate: Polybius' victory narrative may be Fabian whitewash; Philinus (cited at Polybius 1.15) claimed Roman setbacks. The sequence of fighting is uncertain.

events.title: First gladiatorial games at Rome
events.summary: Decimus Junius Brutus Pera and his brother staged three pairs of gladiators in the Forum Boarium at the funeral of their father, the first recorded munus in Rome.
events.detail: The games were a funerary obligation (munus) owed to the dead, an import from Campania or Etruria. The scale grew rapidly: 22 pairs in 216, 25 pairs in 200, 60 pairs over three days in 183, and 120 gladiators at the funeral of P. Licinius Crassus in 183 (Livy 39.46).

events.title: Latin colonies at Firmum and Castrum Novum; Aesernia (263)
events.summary: Rome planted colonies at Firmum and Castrum Novum in Picenum (264) to hold the newly conquered Picentes, and a Latin colony at Aesernia in Samnium (263).
events.detail: Velleius dates Firmum and Castrum Novum to 264 and Aesernia to 263. The Picentes had been crushed in 268, and part of the population transplanted to the Gulf of Salerno (Picentia). Aesernia guarded the upper Volturnus routes into Samnium.
events.note: Castrum Novum's location (Giulianova) is the standard identification; Velleius' dates are the only explicit evidence.

events.title: Alliance with Hiero II; Messalla's sundial
events.summary: After the consul Manius Valerius Maximus marched on Syracuse with four legions, Hiero II made peace, returned prisoners, paid 100 talents and became Rome's loyal ally for the rest of his long life (to 215). Valerius took the cognomen Messalla from Messana.
events.detail: The treaty, at first for 15 years, was made permanent in 248. Hiero's grain supply was crucial to Roman armies in Sicily. Valerius celebrated a triumph and had a painting of his victory placed on the side wall of the Curia Hostilia, the first battle painting displayed in Rome (Pliny 35.22). He also brought back a sundial looted from Catana and set it up in the Forum near the Rostra; Pliny notes it was calibrated for a latitude four degrees south and so told the wrong time for 99 years until Q. Marcius Philippus installed an accurate one in 164.
events.debate: Diodorus gives a different indemnity figure (150,000 drachmas). Pliny's latitude claim for the sundial is approximately right (Catana c. 37.5 N, Rome c. 41.9 N).

events.title: Siege of Agrigentum
events.summary: Both consuls besieged Agrigentum, the main Carthaginian base in Sicily, for about seven months, defeated Hanno's relief army and stormed the town after Hannibal son of Gisco broke out at night. The 25,000 inhabitants were sold into slavery.
events.detail: Hannibal had perhaps 50,000 men in the city; Hanno arrived with 50,000 foot, 6,000 horse and 60 elephants (Polybius 1.18, figures doubted). The Romans were themselves short of food and racked by disease until Hiero kept them supplied. Polybius (1.20.1-2) says the fall of Agrigentum changed Roman war aims: the Senate now hoped to drive Carthage out of Sicily altogether, and decided that this required a fleet.

sides.losses: heavy losses from disease and fighting; Diodorus gives 30,000 foot and 540 horse (implausible)

sides.strength: garrison c. 50,000 (Diodorus) plus Hanno's 50,000 foot, 6,000 horse, 60 elephants

battle.significance: First great Roman success in Sicily; Polybius treats it as the point at which Rome resolved on the conquest of the whole island and the creation of a navy.

events.debate: Diodorus' numbers (probably from Philinus) for both armies and Roman losses are inflated. Polybius' statement about the shift in war aims is often taken as Fabius Pictor's retrospective rationalisation.

events.title: Rome builds its first battle fleet
events.summary: Rome built 100 quinqueremes and 20 triremes, reportedly in sixty days, copying a Carthaginian quinquereme that had run aground. Rowers were trained on benches set up on land.
events.detail: Polybius (1.20-21) tells the story of the stranded Punic ship and the dry-land training. Pliny (16.192) has the whole fleet of Duilius built within 60 days of the timber being felled. The Romans had triremes before (duumviri navales from 311, allied Greek ships), but never a battle fleet of quinqueremes. Punic shipwrecks at Marsala show letters painted on timbers as assembly guides, consistent with mass-production techniques Rome could copy.
events.debate: The 'copy of a single wrecked ship' and the 60-day figure are probably romanticised; Greek allies (socii navales) in Italy surely supplied expertise and crews.

events.title: Battle of the Lipari Islands
events.summary: The consul Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio sailed into Lipara harbour with 17 ships hoping for a betrayal, was trapped by Boodes with 20 Carthaginian ships, and was captured with his whole squadron. The disaster earned him the nickname Asina ('she-ass').
events.detail: Polybius (1.21) says Scipio was taken by a ruse at a parley; Livy's tradition (Per. 17) has him lured by treachery. He was later ransomed or exchanged, triumphed in 254 and was consul again in 254, which shows how little a defeat damaged a noble career.

battle.significance: Humiliating opening for the new Roman navy, quickly reversed at Mylae.

events.title: Battle of Mylae
events.summary: Gaius Duilius defeated a Carthaginian fleet of 130 ships under Hannibal son of Gisco off Mylae, using the corvus boarding bridge to turn sea battle into infantry combat. It was Rome's first naval victory.
events.detail: The corvus (Polybius 1.22) was a boarding bridge about 1.2 m wide and 11 m long, pivoting on a pole in the bow and ending in an iron spike that pinned the enemy deck. The Carthaginians, contemptuous of the clumsy Roman ships, attacked without order, had their first 30 ships grappled and captured, and could not find a safe angle of approach. Polybius gives total Carthaginian losses of about 50 ships; Hannibal escaped in a small boat after his flagship, a 'seven' once owned by Pyrrhus, was taken. Back in Sicily his own officers later crucified him after a further defeat off Sardinia.

sides.losses: c. 50 ships captured or sunk (Polybius); the restored Duilius inscription claims 31 captured and 13 sunk

battle.significance: Proved that Rome could beat Carthage at sea and made Duilius a hero; the corvus dominated the next four years of naval war.

events.debate: The corvus is attested only by Polybius; some scholars think it was less radical than he implies. Steinby argues Rome had more naval experience before 261 than the 'landlubber' tradition allows.

events.title: Duilius' naval triumph and the Columna Rostrata
events.summary: Duilius celebrated the first Roman naval triumph and was honoured with a column decorated with the rams of captured ships in the Forum, and with the lifelong privilege of being escorted home from dinners by a torch-bearer and a flute player.
events.detail: The surviving inscription of the column (CIL I² 25) is an archaising copy of the early Empire, probably Augustan or Claudian, listing ships and huge sums of captured coin; its numerals are heavily restored. Duilius also vowed a temple of Janus in the Forum Holitorium. Cicero (De senectute 44) and Valerius Maximus describe the torch-and-flute honour as unparalleled.
events.debate: Whether the extant inscription faithfully reproduces a 3rd-century text or is a learned imperial reconstruction is debated.

events.title: Battle of Thermae
events.summary: Hamilcar, the Carthaginian commander in Sicily, caught a force of Roman allies separated from the main army near Thermae and killed 4,000-6,000 of them.
events.detail: A reminder that the Carthaginian army in Sicily remained dangerous on land while Rome celebrated Mylae. Polybius gives 4,000 dead; Diodorus 6,000.

battle.significance: Limited, but checked Roman expansion along the north coast.

events.title: Lucius Scipio takes Aleria in Corsica
events.summary: The consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio captured Aleria in Corsica and campaigned against Carthaginian bases in Sardinia. His epitaph in the Tomb of the Scipios boasts 'hec cepit Corsica Aleriaque urbe' and records that he dedicated a temple to the Tempestates (Storms) in thanks for surviving a storm.
events.detail: The elogium (CIL I² 8-9) is one of the earliest substantial Latin inscriptions and a precious contemporary witness. The Corsican expedition shows Rome already taking the war to the islands that fed Carthage's naval network.

events.title: Battle of Sulci
events.summary: The consul Gaius Sulpicius Paterculus defeated the Carthaginian fleet off Sulci in Sardinia. The Carthaginian admiral Hannibal son of Gisco, victor of Lipara and loser at Mylae, was crucified by his own surviving officers.

battle.significance: Ended Hannibal son of Gisco's career and weakened Carthage's hold on Sardinia.

events.title: Calpurnius Flamma's 300 at Camarina
events.summary: When the consul Atilius Calatinus led his army into a defile near Camarina and was trapped, the military tribune Marcus Calpurnius Flamma led 300 volunteers to seize a hill and draw the enemy, allowing the army to escape. Flamma alone survived, found alive under the corpses.
events.detail: Cato in his Origines compared the tribune (whom he called Q. Caedicius) to Leonidas and complained that Greeks got all the glory (Gellius 3.7). The episode shows how Roman exempla of self-sacrifice were constructed and contested within a generation.

sides.strength: 300 volunteers as rearguard of a consular army

battle.significance: Saved a consular army; became a celebrated exemplum of devotio-like sacrifice.

events.debate: The name of the tribune varies: Calpurnius Flamma (Livy, Florus), Q. Caedicius (Cato), Laberius (Claudius Quadrigarius).

events.title: Battle of Tyndaris
events.summary: The consul Gaius Atilius Regulus Serranus, rushing ahead with ten ships, was nearly overwhelmed off Tyndaris but the main Roman fleet came up and sank 8 and captured 10 Carthaginian ships.

battle.significance: Indecisive in strategic terms but encouraged Rome to plan an invasion of Africa.

events.title: Battle of Cape Ecnomus
events.summary: Off the south coast of Sicily the consuls Lucius Manlius Vulso and Marcus Atilius Regulus, carrying an army to invade Africa, fought the Carthaginian fleet of Hamilcar and Hanno. Polybius says 330 Roman ships against 350, perhaps the largest naval battle of antiquity by number of men.
events.detail: The Romans sailed in a wedge of four squadrons, the third towing horse transports. Hamilcar lured the first two squadrons forward while Hanno's right attacked the rear and the Carthaginian left fell on the third squadron. The corvus again told: the Romans sank 30 and captured 64 ships for the loss of 24. Polybius' figure of c. 140,000 Romans and 150,000 Carthaginians (300 rowers and 120 marines per quinquereme) is arithmetic rather than a count.

sides.strength: 350 ships, c. 150,000 men (Polybius) under Hamilcar and Hanno

battle.significance: Opened the way for the first Roman invasion of Africa.

scholarship: Tarn, 'The Fleets of the First Punic War', JHS 27 (1907)
events.debate: Tarn and others think the ship totals inflated or double-counted; the men totals are certainly calculated. Some modern estimates bring each fleet below 250 ships.

events.title: Roman landing at Aspis (Clupea)
events.summary: The Roman army landed at Aspis on the Cape Bon peninsula, took the town and ravaged the rich estates of the Carthaginian hinterland, taking more than 20,000 slaves. On Senate orders Manlius sailed home with most of the fleet, leaving Regulus with 15,000 foot and 500 horse.

events.title: Battle of Adys
events.summary: Regulus defeated a Carthaginian army under Hasdrubal, Bostar and Hamilcar that had unwisely camped on a hill near Adys, where its cavalry and elephants were useless. Regulus then occupied Tunes, within sight of Carthage.
events.detail: Polybius (1.30) blames Carthaginian generalship for the choice of ground. Numidian raiders and a flood of refugees into Carthage brought famine; the city sued for terms.

battle.significance: Brought Carthage to the brink of capitulation in 256.

events.debate: Identification of Adys with Uthina is not secure.

events.title: Regulus' peace terms rejected
events.summary: Regulus, wanting to finish the war before his successor arrived, offered Carthage terms so harsh (evacuation of Sicily and Sardinia, a fleet available to Rome, war indemnity) that the Carthaginians preferred to fight on.
events.detail: Polybius (1.31) says the Carthaginians found the terms worse than defeat. Dio's fragment lists clauses including surrender of all warships but one and payment of Roman war costs.

events.title: Battle of Tunes (Bagradas plain)
events.summary: The Spartan mercenary Xanthippus retrained the Carthaginian army and offered battle on open ground with 12,000 foot, 4,000 cavalry and about 100 elephants. Regulus' army was trampled and enveloped; only about 2,000 men escaped to Aspis and Regulus was captured with 500 others.
events.detail: Polybius (1.32-35) makes Xanthippus the hero and draws the moral that one intelligent man can outweigh numbers. The elephants charged the Roman centre while the superior Carthaginian cavalry drove off the 500 Roman horse and attacked the flanks and rear. Polybius says Xanthippus left Carthage soon afterward; a later story that the jealous Carthaginians drowned him is probably invention.

sides.losses: all but c. 2,000 killed or captured; 500 captured with Regulus

battle.significance: Ended the African invasion; Rome would not return to Africa until Scipio in 204.

events.title: Battle of Cape Hermaeum
events.summary: A Roman fleet of 350 ships under the consuls Servius Fulvius Paetinus Nobilior and Marcus Aemilius Paullus, sent to evacuate the survivors at Aspis, defeated a Carthaginian fleet of 200 off Cape Bon and captured 114 ships with their crews.

battle.significance: A great victory immediately thrown away by the storm off Camarina.

events.title: Fleet destroyed in a storm off Camarina
events.summary: Returning from Africa the Roman fleet, against the advice of its pilots, sailed along the exposed south coast of Sicily in the season of the Orion and Dog Star gales and was wrecked off Camarina: Polybius says only 80 of 364 ships survived.
events.detail: Polybius (1.37) calls it the greatest maritime disaster ever recorded and blames Roman reliance on force rather than seamanship; the top-heavy corvus may have contributed. Losses in men may have approached 100,000 rowers and soldiers, though no ancient figure survives.
events.debate: Some scholars blame the corvus for instability and see its disappearance from the narrative after 255 as a consequence.

events.title: Capture of Panormus
events.summary: A new Roman fleet of 220 ships, built in three months, carried the consuls Aulus Atilius Calatinus and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina to Panormus, which they stormed. 14,000 inhabitants ransomed themselves at two minae each; 13,000 were sold.

battle.significance: Gave Rome the chief port of north-western Sicily.

events.title: Second storm disaster off Cape Palinurus
events.summary: Returning from a raid on the African coast, the Roman fleet was caught by a storm off Cape Palinurus in Lucania and lost about 150 ships. The Senate for a time limited the navy to 60 ships to guard the coasts.

events.title: Censors degrade 400 equites
events.summary: The censors Manius Valerius Maximus and Publius Sempronius Sophus deprived 400 equites of their public horses for refusing orders to work on fortifications in Sicily, and reduced them to aerarii.

events.title: Battle of Panormus
events.summary: Lucius Caecilius Metellus, holding Panormus, provoked Hasdrubal's army to the walls, then had light troops shower the elephants with missiles from the ditch. The maddened beasts turned on their own lines, and a sally completed the rout. Many elephants were captured.
events.detail: Polybius (1.40) emphasises the planning: skirmishers sheltered by the ditch and a supply of javelins from the walls. The battle ended Roman fear of elephants, which had lingered since Pyrrhus and Tunes.

sides.strength: a consular army, perhaps 2 legions and allies
army under Hasdrubal with c. 100-140 elephants

battle.significance: Last major land battle of the war in Sicily; confined Carthage to Lilybaeum and Drepana.

events.debate: Elephant numbers vary: Pliny gives 142 (or 140) elephants paraded at Rome, other figures range from 104 to 120. Date sometimes put in 251; Polybius' chronology favours 250.

events.title: Metellus' triumph with captured elephants
events.summary: Metellus shipped the captured elephants across the Straits on rafts made of jars and paraded them in his triumph; they were then killed with javelins in the Circus Maximus. The elephant became a hereditary emblem on coins of the Caecilii Metelli.
events.detail: Pliny (8.16-17) preserves the competing accounts of Verrius Flaccus and Lucius Piso on their fate. Metellus, later pontifex maximus, lost his sight rescuing the Palladium when the temple of Vesta burned in 241.

events.title: Embassy and death of Regulus
events.summary: According to Roman tradition the captive Regulus was sent to Rome on parole to negotiate an exchange of prisoners, advised the Senate to refuse, kept his oath by returning to Carthage, and was tortured to death.
events.detail: Polybius, who uses Regulus as an exemplum of the fickleness of fortune, says nothing of the embassy or the torture. Diodorus (24.12) reports that Regulus' widow, given two Carthaginian prisoners, tortured them so savagely that the tribunes intervened; many scholars think the torture story was invented to excuse her. The legend was canonised by Cicero (De officiis 3.99-115) and Horace (Odes 3.5).
events.debate: Polybius' silence is the strongest argument against the embassy; the torture story is widely regarded as Roman propaganda or family apologetic.

events.title: Siege of Lilybaeum
events.summary: Rome besieged Lilybaeum, the strongest Carthaginian fortress in Sicily, by land and sea from 250 until the end of the war. The garrison under Himilco held out, supplied by blockade runners such as Hannibal 'the Rhodian', whose fast quadrireme ran in and out of the harbour in daylight until it was captured.
events.detail: The Romans built siege works and rams; Himilco burned them in a gale-driven night sortie. The captured ship of the Rhodian became the template for the Roman fleet that won at the Aegates in 241 (Polybius 1.59.8). Excavations at Marsala have exposed the great Punic walls and ditch and the remains of Punic warships.

sides.strength: both consular armies in 250 (110,000 by Diodorus, impossible) and a fleet of 200

battle.significance: Tied down Roman forces for nine years; the town surrendered only under the peace of 241.

events.title: Battle of Drepana
events.summary: The consul Publius Claudius Pulcher attempted a surprise attack on the Carthaginian fleet in Drepana harbour. Adherbal slipped out, caught the Romans strung out against the shore and destroyed the fleet: 93 Roman ships were taken and only about 30 escaped with Claudius.
events.detail: This was Rome's only major defeat at sea in the war. The tradition, unknown to Polybius, says that when the sacred chickens refused to eat before the battle Claudius threw them overboard: 'Let them drink, since they will not eat'.

battle.significance: Destroyed Roman naval power for the time being; combined with the storm at Phintias it left Rome almost without a fleet until 242.

events.title: Trial of Claudius Pulcher and the dictatorship of Claudius Glicia
events.summary: Recalled after Drepana, Claudius Pulcher mocked the order to appoint a dictator by naming his freedman clerk Marcus Claudius Glicia, who was forced to resign. Prosecuted for perduellio by tribunes, Claudius was fined 120,000 asses. In 246 his sister Claudia, jostled by the crowd at the games, wished her brother were alive to lose another fleet and thin the mob; she was fined by the aediles.

events.title: Battle of Phintias and the storm off Pachynus
events.summary: Carthalo attacked a Roman supply convoy of about 120 warships and 800 transports under the consul Lucius Junius Pullus near Phintias, then manoeuvred so that a southerly gale struck the Romans on the lee shore near Camarina and Pachynus. Almost the entire fleet was wrecked.
events.detail: Pullus salvaged his reputation by seizing the summit and temple of Venus Erycina on Mount Eryx. He was later prosecuted; tradition says he killed himself before trial. With Drepana, 249 was the worst year of the war for the Roman navy.

sides.strength: c. 120 warships, 800 transports under L. Junius Pullus

battle.significance: Left Rome with almost no fleet for six years.

events.title: Atilius Calatinus, first dictator to command outside Italy
events.summary: After the Glicia fiasco Aulus Atilius Calatinus was named dictator and led an army to Sicily, the first time a dictator commanded outside Italy.
events.detail: Calatinus was a hero of the war (triumph 257, consul 258 and 254). His elogium on the Via Appia boasted that most peoples agreed he was the foremost man of Rome (Cicero, De senectute 61).

events.title: First Ludi Tarentini (Secular Games)
events.summary: Amid war disasters and portents, the Sibylline Books prescribed nocturnal sacrifices to Dis Pater and Proserpina at the Tarentum in the Campus Martius, to be repeated every hundred years. Varro regarded this as the first celebration of the Ludi Saeculares.
events.detail: The next celebration fell in 146 or 149 (sources disagree). Augustus' Ludi Saeculares of 17 BC reworked the ritual into a festival of renewal.
events.debate: Whether there were earlier Secular Games (509, 449, 348 per the quindecimviral commentarii) is disputed; most scholars accept 249 as the first historical celebration.

events.title: Hamilcar Barca at Heircte
events.summary: Hamilcar Barca took command in Sicily and seized Heircte, a fortified height near Panormus with its own anchorage, from which he raided the Italian coast as far as Cumae and harried Roman forces for three years.
events.detail: Polybius (1.56) describes Heircte as a steep-sided plateau with arable land and a harbour, usually identified with Monte Pellegrino. In 244 Hamilcar moved by sea to Eryx. Hannibal, his eldest son, was born about this time.
events.debate: Heircte has also been placed at Monte Castellaccio; Polybius' description fits Pellegrino better.

events.title: Maritime colonies at Alsium (247) and Fregenae (245)
events.summary: Two small citizen colonies of about 300 families each were planted on the Etruscan coast west of Rome to guard against Carthaginian raids such as those launched by Hamilcar from Sicily.

events.title: Latin colony at Brundisium
events.summary: A Latin colony was founded at Brundisium, the best harbour of the Adriatic coast and the future gateway to Greece and the East.

events.title: Hamilcar holds Eryx
events.summary: Hamilcar seized the town of Eryx halfway up the mountain, between a Roman garrison on the summit (holding the temple of Venus Erycina) and a Roman army at its foot. Besieger and besieged at once, he held the position for three years until ordered to make peace.
events.detail: Polybius (1.58) compares the duel to two boxers in perfect condition fighting to exhaustion. Some Gallic mercenaries of Hamilcar deserted to the Romans and were later used to garrison the temple, which they plundered.

sides.strength: garrison on summit and army at foot

battle.significance: Hamilcar was undefeated in Sicily, a fact central to Barcid pride and resentment after 241.

events.title: Citizens fund a new fleet
events.summary: With the treasury exhausted, wealthy Romans singly or in groups of two or three each undertook to build and equip a quinquereme, to be repaid only if the war was won. Some 200 ships were built on the model of the Rhodian's captured blockade runner.
events.detail: Polybius (1.59) presents this as patriotic generosity; modern scholars see it as a loan by the rich with victory as collateral, and an early sign of the financial capacity of Rome's propertied class.

events.title: Creation of the second praetorship (praetor peregrinus)
events.summary: A second praetor was created, who came to deal with legal cases involving foreigners (inter peregrinos), leaving the praetor urbanus for citizens. The new office also supplied an additional holder of imperium for war.
events.detail: The title praetor peregrinus is later; the original designation was 'qui inter peregrinos ius dicit'. The new praetor Quintus Valerius Falto served at the Aegates in 241.
events.debate: Some argue the jurisdictional distinction emerged gradually and that in 242 the motive was simply military.

events.title: Battle of the Aegates Islands
events.summary: Gaius Lutatius Catulus and the praetor Quintus Valerius Falto, with 200 newly built quinqueremes, intercepted a hastily manned Carthaginian relief fleet under Hanno west of Sicily as it tried to reach Hamilcar at Eryx. The heavily laden Punic ships were routed: 50 sunk and 70 captured with nearly 10,000 men. Carthage sued for peace.
events.detail: Lutatius trained his crews for months and chose to fight in a stiff westerly that favoured the Carthaginians' approach, because the Punic ships were weighed down with grain for Eryx and had raw crews. Hanno was crucified at Carthage. Since 2004 underwater survey by the Soprintendenza del Mare and the RPM Nautical Foundation off the north-west of Levanzo has recovered more than twenty bronze rams, helmets and amphorae from the battlefield; several rams carry Latin inscriptions naming quaestors who approved them, and some are Punic, giving direct archaeological confirmation of the battle and of ram sizes.

battle.significance: Decided the First Punic War.

scholarship: Tusa & Royal, 'The landscape of the naval battle at the Egadi Islands (241 B.C.)', JRA 25 (2012)
events.debate: Valerius Maximus records a legal dispute between Lutatius and Valerius Falto over who deserved the triumph; both ultimately triumphed. Date 10 March is from the Fasti (Eutropius); the Roman calendar was then roughly in step with the seasons.

events.title: Treaty of Lutatius
events.summary: Carthage agreed to evacuate Sicily, not to make war on Hiero or his allies, return all Roman prisoners without ransom and pay 2,200 Euboic talents over twenty years. The Roman assembly rejected Lutatius' draft; a commission of ten raised the indemnity to 3,200 talents, 1,000 at once and the rest in ten years, and added the islands between Sicily and Italy.
events.detail: Polybius (1.62-63, 3.27) gives the terms in detail. Western Sicily became Rome's first overseas possession, initially supervised by quaestors and later (from 227) governed by a praetor; Hiero's kingdom in the east remained independent. Polybius calculates that over the war Rome lost about 700 quinqueremes and Carthage 500.

events.title: Revolt and destruction of Falerii
events.summary: The Falisci rebelled immediately after the war and were crushed in six days by both consuls. Half their territory was confiscated and the hill town (Falerii Veteres, Civita Castellana) was abandoned for a new, less defensible site in the plain, Falerii Novi, whose walls still stand.

battle.significance: Last revolt of an Etruscan-area community for a century; the relocation of Falerii is archaeologically visible.

events.note: The Falisci are not separately listed as a polity; they appear here under rome as rebel allies.

events.title: Creation of the last two tribes: Velina and Quirina
events.summary: The censors created the tribus Velina and Quirina for citizens settled in Picenum and the Sabine country, bringing the number of tribes to 35. No further tribes were ever created; later citizens were enrolled in existing ones.

events.title: Reform of the comitia centuriata
events.summary: Between the First and Second Punic Wars the centuriate assembly was reorganised to align its centuries with the 35 tribes: each tribe supplied two centuries (seniores, iuniores) of each of five property classes. The first class lost its outright majority, and the right of the prerogative century passed to a century chosen by lot.
events.detail: Livy (1.43.12-13) and Cicero (De re publica 2.39) are the main evidence; the Tabula Hebana of AD 19 shows how the system worked in practice. The date, extent and exact arithmetic (373 centuries?) are uncertain; the reform is often attributed to the censors of 241 or to Gaius Flaminius (censor 220).

events.title: Outbreak of the Mercenary (Truceless) War
events.summary: About 20,000 mercenaries evacuated from Sicily mutinied at Sicca over arrears of pay. Led by Spendius, a runaway Campanian slave, and Mathos, a Libyan, they seized the Carthaginian envoy Gisco and raised the Libyan countryside, beginning a savage three-year war that nearly destroyed Carthage.
events.detail: Polybius (1.65-88) treats the war as a lesson in the dangers of mercenary armies and calls it 'truceless' (aspondos) for its atrocities. Rome scrupulously refused requests from Utica and the rebels and allowed Carthage to buy supplies in Italy, until the affair of Sardinia in 238.

events.title: Battle of the Saw
events.summary: Hamilcar Barca trapped a rebel army of some 40,000 under Spendius in a saw-shaped range of hills, the Prion, starved it into cannibalism and annihilated it after seizing its leaders at a parley.
events.detail: Polybius (1.85) says the trapped men ate their prisoners and slaves. Mathos was defeated later in 238 and paraded through Carthage before execution.

sides.strength: c. 10,000 plus Numidian allies under Naravas

battle.significance: Broke the rebellion; restored Hamilcar's political dominance at Carthage.

events.title: Rome seizes Sardinia
events.summary: When mercenaries in Sardinia revolted and invited Rome in, Rome accepted. Carthage prepared to reconquer the island; Rome declared war, and exhausted Carthage surrendered Sardinia and paid an additional 1,200 talents (238/237).
events.detail: Polybius (3.28) condemns the seizure as without any pretext or justification and calls it the chief cause of the Second Punic War, since it fuelled the anger of Hamilcar and the Barcids. Corsica followed. Conquest of the Sardinian interior took decades (campaigns 235-231, revolts in 215 and 177-176).
scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
events.debate: Polybius' unusually harsh verdict on Rome is a key text for the imperialism debate: Harris sees here naked aggression; Hoyos and Eckstein emphasise opportunism in a lawless interstate system.

events.title: Institution of the Floralia; Clivus Publicius
events.summary: The plebeian aediles Lucius and Marcus Publicius Malleolus used fines from graziers who had encroached on public land to found a temple of Flora near the Circus Maximus and to build the Clivus Publicius up the Aventine. The Ludi Florales became annual in 173.

events.title: Hamilcar Barca goes to Spain; Hannibal's oath
events.summary: Hamilcar sailed to Gades and began building a Carthaginian dominion in southern Spain, rich in silver mines and manpower. Before leaving he made his nine-year-old son Hannibal swear on an altar never to be a friend of the Romans.
events.detail: Hannibal told the oath story himself to Antiochus III in 193 (Polybius 3.11). Fabius Pictor alleged that the Barcids acted independently of the Carthaginian government; Polybius (3.8) rejects this. The Spanish venture paid the Roman indemnity and created the army of Hannibal.
events.debate: 'Wrath of the Barcids' (Polybius 3.9-10) versus a state enterprise of Carthage: Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty, argues for a Barcid regime working with, not against, the home government.

events.title: First triumph on the Alban Mount
events.summary: Refused a triumph by the Senate for his Corsican campaign, the consul Gaius Papirius Maso held one on his own authority on the Alban Mount, wearing a myrtle crown instead of laurel. The precedent was followed by Marcellus in 211 and others.

events.title: Temple of Janus closed
events.summary: The consul Titus Manlius Torquatus closed the doors of the temple of Janus, signifying that Rome was at peace, for the first time since King Numa. The peace lasted only months.

events.title: Lex Flaminia de agro Gallico viritim dividundo
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Flaminius, against strong senatorial opposition, carried a plebiscite distributing the ager Gallicus (land taken from the Senones in 283) in individual allotments to Roman citizens rather than founding colonies.
events.detail: Polybius (2.21) regards the law as the beginning of the 'corruption of the people' and a direct cause of the Gallic invasion of 225, because the Boii feared that Rome intended their extermination. Cicero says Flaminius' own father dragged him from the rostra; he persisted. The law made Flaminius a popular hero and a senatorial bête noire.
scholarship: Feig Vishnia, State, Society and Popular Leaders in Mid-Republican Rome (1996)
events.debate: Polybius dates it to 232; Cicero to 228 (consulship of Sp. Carvilius). Modern scholars debate whether it was a 'popularis' measure in the later sense.

events.title: Death of Hamilcar Barca
events.summary: Hamilcar drowned while retreating across a river during the siege of Helice, according to Diodorus by the treachery of the Oretani king. His son-in-law Hasdrubal the Fair succeeded to the command.
events.debate: Helice is variously placed at Elche (Ilici) or Elche de la Sierra; the date may be winter 229/228.

events.title: Murder of a Roman envoy by the Illyrians
events.summary: Responding to Italian traders' complaints of Illyrian piracy, Rome sent Gaius and Lucius Coruncanius to Queen Teuta, regent of the Ardiaean kingdom. Polybius says Teuta replied that it was not the custom of Illyrian kings to stop their subjects plundering at sea; one envoy spoke insolently and was murdered on the way home.
events.detail: Teuta's fleets had sacked Phoenice in Epirus (230) and were besieging Issa. The murder gave Rome its casus belli. Appian has a different story, in which Issa appealed to Rome.
events.debate: Polybius' account emphasises Illyrian piracy; Appian and Dio make the appeal of Issa central. Modern scholars (Derow, Eckstein) debate whether protection of traders was a real motive.

events.title: Battle of Paxos
events.summary: An Illyrian fleet with Acarnanian allies defeated the combined fleet of the Achaean and Aetolian Leagues off the island of Paxos. The Illyrians lashed their lembi together in fours to snare the enemy ships, then boarded. Corcyra surrendered to Demetrius of Pharos.

sides.losses: 4 quadriremes and a quinquereme lost; Margos of Caryneia killed

battle.significance: Showed the Greek leagues could not check Illyrian sea power; Rome intervened weeks later.

events.title: First Roman army crosses the Adriatic
events.summary: The consul Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus with 200 ships and Aulus Postumius Albinus with 20,000 foot and 2,000 horse crossed to Illyria. Demetrius of Pharos betrayed Corcyra to them; Apollonia, Epidamnus and the Parthini and Atintani surrendered into Roman fides, and the siege of Issa was raised.
events.detail: This was the first Roman army in the Balkans. The communities that placed themselves under Roman protection formed a loose Roman sphere, not a province, which later gave Philip V cause for hostility.
scholarship: Hammond, 'Illyris, Rome and Macedon in 229-205 BC', JRS 58 (1968)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
events.debate: Whether this created a Roman 'protectorate' (Badian, Hammond) or merely informal friendships (Gruen, Eckstein) is central to debates on Roman policy in the East.

events.title: Peace with Teuta and Roman embassies to Greece
events.summary: Teuta agreed to pay tribute, give up most of Illyria to Demetrius and others, and not sail south of Lissus with more than two lembi, and those unarmed. Rome sent envoys to the Aetolian and Achaean Leagues to explain its actions; Corinth admitted Romans to the Isthmian Games.

events.title: Gauls and Greeks buried alive in the Forum Boarium
events.summary: On the instruction of the Sibylline Books, a Gallic man and woman and a Greek man and woman were buried alive in the Forum Boarium to avert a prophecy that Gauls and Greeks would occupy Rome. The rite was repeated after Cannae (216) and in 114/113.
events.detail: Livy (22.57.6) calls the rite 'minime Romanum'. It is the clearest case of human sacrifice at Rome and was performed in a stone chamber; Plutarch and Pliny show sacrifices at the spot were still offered in their day.
events.debate: The date of the first occasion is given variously as 228, 226 or 225; it is linked to fear of the Gallic invasion.

events.title: Two new praetors for Sicily and Sardinia-Corsica
events.summary: The number of praetors was raised from two to four so that annual magistrates could govern Sicily and Sardinia-Corsica. Gaius Flaminius was the first praetor in Sicily and Marcus Valerius in Sardinia. This is usually taken as the formal beginning of the Roman province system.
events.detail: 'Provincia' originally meant a sphere of command, not a territory; the regular dispatch of a praetor marks the transition. Sicily paid a tithe on grain on the model of Hiero's lex Hieronica; the system was formalised later.

events.title: Hasdrubal founds New Carthage
events.summary: Hasdrubal the Fair founded Qart Hadasht ('New City', Carthago Nova) on a superb defensible harbour in south-east Spain, near silver mines that employed 40,000 workers in Polybius' day. He married an Iberian princess and was acclaimed as general by the Spanish peoples.

events.title: The Ebro Treaty
events.summary: Worried by the Gallic threat, Rome sent envoys to Hasdrubal, who undertook not to cross the Iber (Ebro) under arms. Nothing was said of the rest of Spain.
events.detail: Polybius (2.13; 3.27) is the sole detailed source. Saguntum, south of the Ebro, was at some point taken into Roman friendship; whether before or after the treaty, and whether the treaty implicitly protected it, became the legal dispute of 219-218. Appian wrongly places Saguntum north of the river.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)
events.debate: Some scholars (Carcopino) proposed that 'Iber' meant a more southerly river such as the Júcar, putting Saguntum north of the line; this is generally rejected. The treaty may have been a personal undertaking by Hasdrubal never ratified at Carthage.

events.title: Battle of Faesulae
events.summary: A huge Gallic army of Boii, Insubres and Gaesatae from beyond the Alps (Polybius: 50,000 foot, 20,000 horse and chariots) invaded Etruria, plundering towards Rome. Near Faesulae, pretending to retreat at night, it ambushed a Roman praetorian army and killed 6,000.
events.detail: The survivors were rescued by the arrival of the consul Lucius Aemilius Papus. The Gauls, laden with plunder, decided to withdraw along the coast.

sides.strength: praetor's army of Etruscans and Sabines

battle.significance: Deepest Gallic penetration since 390; heightened Roman panic.

events.debate: Polybius' 'Faesulae' may be a corruption for Clusium; the location is uncertain.

events.title: Rome's manpower register of 225
events.summary: In alarm at the Gallic invasion, Rome and its allies drew up lists of men capable of bearing arms. Polybius, probably from Fabius Pictor who served in the war, gives a total of over 700,000 foot and 70,000 horse.
events.detail: The list (Polybius 2.24) breaks the total down by people: Romans and Campanians 250,000 foot and 23,000 horse; Latins 80,000 and 5,000; Samnites 70,000 and 7,000; and so on. It is the single most important document for the demography of Roman Italy and the scale of Rome's military resources against Hannibal.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)
events.debate: Brunt showed that Polybius' arithmetic contains double counting and that the figures are of varying kinds (men under arms vs registered). Their interpretation underlies the 'low count' vs 'high count' debate on Italian population.

events.title: Battle of Telamon
events.summary: Retreating along the Etruscan coast, the Gallic army was caught between the consul Gaius Atilius Regulus, who had just landed at Pisa from Sardinia, and Lucius Aemilius Papus following behind. Fighting back to back, the Gauls were annihilated: 40,000 killed and 10,000 captured, including the king Concolitanus. Aneroestes fled and killed himself.
events.detail: Polybius' description (2.27-31) is vivid: the naked Gaesatae in the front ranks, the gold torques and armlets, the trumpets and horns, the Roman javelins against the small Gallic shields, and the slashing Gallic swords that bent after a blow. Atilius was killed early in a cavalry fight for a hill and his head carried to the Gallic kings. Aemilius Papus triumphed and dedicated the standards on the Capitol.

sides.strength: two consular armies, c. 40,000 under C. Atilius Regulus and L. Aemilius Papus
c. 50,000-70,000 Boii, Insubres, Taurisci and Gaesatae

battle.significance: Ended the last great Gallic invasion of peninsular Italy and opened the conquest of the Po valley.

scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957)

events.title: Boii submit
events.summary: The consuls Quintus Fulvius Flaccus and Titus Manlius Torquatus invaded Boian territory, the first Roman army to campaign north of the Apennines in strength, and forced the Boii to submit.

events.title: Flaminius defeats the Insubres
events.summary: The consuls Gaius Flaminius and Publius Furius Philus crossed the Po and defeated the Insubres. The military tribunes ordered the front ranks to use their thrusting spears to absorb the first Gallic sword blows before closing with swords. Flaminius, who had ignored a Senate letter recalling him over bad omens, triumphed by popular vote.
events.detail: Polybius (2.32-33) credits the victory to the tribunes and blames Flaminius for fighting with a river at his back. The hostile tradition (Plutarch, Marcellus 4) says the Senate refused the triumph and Flaminius and Furius were forced to abdicate.

sides.strength: two consular armies with Cenomani allies

battle.significance: First major Roman victory north of the Po.

events.debate: Polybius' hostility to Flaminius (via Fabius Pictor) colours the account; Livy and Plutarch preserve contradictory traditions about the triumph.

events.title: Battle of Clastidium
events.summary: While his colleague Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio besieged Acerrae, the consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus led cavalry to relieve Clastidium, besieged by Insubres and Gaesatae. He killed the Gallic king Viridomarus in single combat and dedicated his armour to Jupiter Feretrius, the third and last spolia opima of the Republic.
events.detail: Only Romulus and Aulus Cornelius Cossus (437 or 426) were credited with spolia opima before. The poet Naevius wrote a historical play, Clastidium, on the victory, probably for Marcellus' funeral games in 208. Coins of a later Marcellinus (RRC 439/1, c. 50 BC) show Marcellus carrying the spoils into the temple.

battle.significance: Broke the Insubrian resistance; made Marcellus a heroic figure.

events.title: Capture of Mediolanum and submission of the Insubres
events.summary: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus captured Acerrae and then Mediolanum, the chief town of the Insubres, who surrendered. Within four years Rome planted colonies at Placentia and Cremona to hold the line of the Po.

battle.significance: Completed the first conquest of the Insubres, undone by Hannibal's arrival in 218.

events.title: First Istrian War
events.summary: The consuls Marcus Minucius Rufus and Publius Cornelius Scipio Asina subdued the Istrians, accused of piracy against Roman grain ships.

events.title: Assassination of Hasdrubal; Hannibal takes command
events.summary: Hasdrubal the Fair was killed at night in his house by a Celt with a private grievance (Livy: a slave avenging his master). The army acclaimed the 25-year-old Hannibal as general, confirmed by the assembly at Carthage.

events.title: Censorship of Flaminius: Via Flaminia and Circus Flaminius
events.summary: As censor, Gaius Flaminius built the Via Flaminia from Rome across the Apennines to Ariminum and the Circus Flaminius in the Campus Martius, where the Ludi Plebeii were held. He also restricted freedmen to the four urban tribes.
events.detail: The road tied the ager Gallicus and the new northern frontier directly to Rome; the circus became a key public space for triumphal assemblies and later temples (Hercules Musarum, Juno Regina).
events.locName: Circus Flaminius, Rome / Via Flaminia to Ariminum
events.debate: The circus may date to 221 and is sometimes attributed to Flaminius' consulship; the road's route was later rebuilt by Augustus.

events.title: Battle of the Tagus
events.summary: Returning from a raid deep into the territory of the Vaccaei (taking Helmantica and Arbucala), Hannibal was attacked at the Tagus by the Carpetani with Olcades and Vaccaei. He let them begin to cross the river and slaughtered them in the water with cavalry and elephants.
events.detail: Polybius' figure of 100,000 enemies is clearly inflated. The campaign brought central Spain under Carthaginian control and left only Saguntum outside it south of the Ebro.

battle.significance: Secured Hannibal's base in central Iberia before the war with Rome.

events.title: Second Illyrian War: Dimale and Pharos
events.summary: Demetrius of Pharos had sailed beyond Lissus with 50 lembi and raided the Aegean. The consuls Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Marcus Livius Salinator took his fortress of Dimale in seven days, then captured Pharos by landing a decoy force in the harbour while the main army hid in a wooded hollow. Demetrius fled to Philip V.
events.detail: Demetrius became an adviser to Philip and, according to Polybius, urged him to fight Rome. Livius Salinator was convicted after his triumph of unfair division of the booty and withdrew from public life until 210, a grudge that resurfaced in his censorship with Claudius Nero in 204.

battle.significance: Ended Demetrius' bid for Adriatic power; pushed him into Philip V's camp, a link in the chain to the First Macedonian War.

scholarship: Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
events.debate: Whether Rome fought this war to secure its rear before the expected Punic conflict (Polybius 3.16) or as a reaction to Demetrius' provocations is debated.
